title: Analytics Engineering with dbt and DuckDB
subtitle: Turn raw data into tested, documented models with dbt Core and DuckDB: sources, staging, marts, tests, snapshots, incremental models and CI.
outcomes: Set up a dbt project on DuckDB, and build models that depend on each other with ref
Declare sources with freshness checks, load seeds, and write staging, intermediate and mart models
Write reusable SQL with Jinja and macros, and select parts of the graph to build
Test models with generic, singular and unit tests, and document them with a lineage graph
Keep history with snapshots and build large tables incrementally, safely
Run dbt in CI with targets, state selection and a GitHub Actions workflow
prerequisites: SQL as in SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip (joins, GROUP BY, CTEs and window functions) and Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines (ELT and idempotent loads), or the same skills. Install Python 3.10 or later and, in a virtual environment, python -m pip install dbt-core dbt-duckdb (tested with dbt-core 1.12.6 and dbt-duckdb 1.11.0). Git and a GitHub account help with the CI lab.
description:
Analytics engineers turn raw tables into the clean, trusted models that dashboards, analysts and machine learning depend on, and dbt is the tool most of them use to do it. In this course you'll build a dbt project for a city bike-share scheme on DuckDB, a free database that runs on your laptop: load raw trips and members, declare them as sources with freshness checks, add stations as a seed, and layer staging, intermediate and mart models with ref, Jinja and macros.

Then you'll make the project trustworthy and ready for production: generic, singular and unit tests that catch the duplicated trip, the trip that ends before it starts and the vehicle type no one expected; documentation with a lineage graph; snapshots that keep members' history; an incremental fact table that picks up late data; and CI with separate targets, state selection and a GitHub Actions workflow. Every lab uses real output from dbt Core 1.12, and the capstone models a football club's ticket sales from scratch. Data Warehousing and Dimensional Modelling covers the design of marts in depth, and Orchestrating Data Pipelines with Apache Airflow shows how to schedule dbt alongside other jobs.

modules.title: Analytics engineering and your first dbt project
modules.summary: What analytics engineering is and where dbt fits, how a dbt project and its profile are set up, and how models, ref and materialisations work.

lessons.title: What analytics engineering is
objectives: Explain what analytics engineers do, and how dbt fits into ELT
Install dbt Core with the DuckDB adapter
key_points: Analytics engineering turns raw data in the warehouse into clean, tested, documented tables that analysts and dashboards can trust, with software practices: version control, code review, automated tests and CI.
dbt handles the T in ELT: each model is a SELECT statement in a .sql file, and dbt wraps it in the SQL that creates a view or table, builds models in dependency order, and tests and documents them.

dbt Core is the open-source command-line tool; it talks to a warehouse through an adapter, such as dbt-duckdb, dbt-postgres, dbt-snowflake or dbt-bigquery, and dbt Labs also sells a hosted platform for developing and scheduling projects.

pip install dbt-core dbt-duckdb installs dbt Core 1.x (1.12 in this course). The separate dbt package on PyPI is dbt v2, which dbt's installer now offers by default for new installations, with an upgrade guide for v1 projects.
dbt doesn't extract or load data: an ingestion tool or script lands the raw tables first (here load_raw.py), and dbt transforms them inside the warehouse.

lessons.title: Projects, profiles and targets
objectives: Describe the files of a dbt project and its profile
Check a project's set-up with dbt debug
key_points: A dbt project is a folder with dbt_project.yml (the project's name, the profile it uses, its folder paths and default configs) and folders for models, seeds, tests, macros and snapshots.

profiles.yml says where to build: a profile has targets such as dev and ci, each with an adapter type and connection settings; for dbt-duckdb, that's the path of the database file and a number of threads.

dbt looks for profiles.yml in the current folder first and then in ~/.dbt/, unless --profiles-dir or DBT_PROFILES_DIR points elsewhere; read secrets with {{ env_var('NAME') }} instead of writing them in.
dbt debug checks the project file, the profile and the connection and ends with All checks passed!; dbt init creates a new project and helps write its profile.
Folder-level configs in dbt_project.yml, such as +materialized: view under staging, apply to every model in that folder; a config() block or a properties file can override them for one model.

lessons.title: Models, ref and materialisations
objectives: Write models that build on each other with ref
Choose a materialisation for each model
key_points: A model is a .sql file holding one SELECT, named after the file; {{ ref('stg_trips') }} refers to another model, and dbt swaps in the right relation name and uses every ref to build the dependency graph (DAG).

Materialisations decide what dbt builds: view (the default), table, incremental (adds or updates rows instead of rebuilding) and ephemeral (inlined into other models as a CTE); set them in dbt_project.yml or with {{ config(materialized='table') }}.
dbt run builds models in dependency order, running independent ones in parallel threads; dbt build also loads seeds, takes snapshots and runs tests, each test straight after the model it checks.
dbt compiles Jinja into plain SQL first: target/compiled holds the SELECT each model became and target/run the statements dbt ran, which is where to look when a model fails.
dbt show --select model, or --inline "select ...", previews query results without building anything, and dbt ls lists the project's resources, both handy for checking work.

files.content:
name: bikeshare
version: "1.0.0"
profile: bikeshare  # the profile in profiles.yml that says where to build

model-paths: ["models"]
seed-paths: ["seeds"]
test-paths: ["tests"]
macro-paths: ["macros"]
snapshot-paths: ["snapshots"]
clean-targets: ["target", "dbt_packages"]

models:
  bikeshare:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
    marts:
      +materialized: table

# dbt looks for profiles.yml in the current folder first, then in ~/.dbt/.
bikeshare:
  target: dev
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: duckdb
      path: bikeshare.duckdb  # the same file load_raw.py writes to
      threads: 4

"""Load synthetic bike-share data into the raw schema of a DuckDB database, as an ingestion tool would.

    python load_raw.py               batch 1: trips for 1-7 May 2024, and the members table as it is on 7 May
    python load_raw.py --batch 2     batch 2: trips for 8 May (and one late trip from the 7th), updated members
    python load_raw.py --db ci.duckdb   load into another database file

raw.trips is appended to; raw.members is replaced with the source's current state. Every row gets _loaded_at,
the time it was loaded. Only random.random() is used, so the data is the same on every computer.
"""

import argparse
import math
import random
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

import duckdb

STATIONS = [f"S{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 13)]
WEIGHTS = [4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1]  # the centre is busiest


def pick(rng, items, weights=None):
    weights = weights or [1] * len(items)
    x = rng.random() * sum(weights)
    for item, w in zip(items, weights):
        x -= w
        if x < 0:
            return item
    return items[-1]


def members(rng, batch):
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, 151):
        joined = date(2023, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=int(rng.random() * 485))
        plan = pick(rng, ["annual", "monthly", "student"], [50, 35, 15])
        rows.append([f"M{i:03d}", str(joined), plan, f"{joined} 00:00:00"])
    if batch == 2:
        for r in rows[6::17]:  # nine members change plan on 8 May
            r[2] = {"monthly": "annual", "student": "monthly", "annual": "monthly"}[r[2]]
            r[3] = "2024-05-08 06:00:00"
        rows.append(["M151", "2024-05-08", "monthly", "2024-05-08 09:30:00"])
    return rows


def trips(rng, days, first_id):
    rows, n = [], first_id
    for day in days:
        for _ in range(180 + int(rng.random() * 50)):
            start = datetime(day.year, day.month, day.day, 6) + timedelta(seconds=int(rng.random() * 61200))
            minutes = 3 + min(-math.log(1 - rng.random()) * 11, 60)
            member = f"M{int(rng.random() * 150) + 1:03d}" if rng.random() < 0.8 else None
            rows.append([f"T{n:06d}", member, pick(rng, STATIONS, WEIGHTS), pick(rng, STATIONS, WEIGHTS),
                         f"{start:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}", f"{start + timedelta(seconds=int(minutes * 60)):%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}",
                         "electric" if rng.random() < 0.35 else "classic"])
            n += 1
    return rows


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--batch", type=int, choices=[1, 2], default=1)
    parser.add_argument("--db", default="bikeshare.duckdb")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    rng = random.Random(2024)
    batch1 = trips(rng, [date(2024, 5, d) for d in range(1, 8)], 1)
    batch1.append(batch1[122][:])  # T000123 is delivered twice
    batch1[455][5] = batch1[455][4][:11] + "07:00:00"  # T000456 ends before it starts
    batch1[455][4] = batch1[455][4][:11] + "07:05:00"
    batch1[788][6] = "Scooter"  # T000789: a vehicle type the source has just started sending
    if args.batch == 1:
        new_trips, member_rows = batch1, members(random.Random(7), 1)
    else:
        new_trips = trips(random.Random(8), [date(2024, 5, 8)], len(batch1) + 1)
        new_trips.append([f"T{len(batch1) + len(new_trips) + 1:06d}", "M042", "S03", "S01", "2024-05-07 23:52:10",
                          "2024-05-08 00:04:40", "classic"])  # a trip from the 7th that arrived late
        member_rows = members(random.Random(7), 2)
    loaded_at = datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)  # one load time for the whole batch
    con = duckdb.connect(args.db)
    con.execute("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS raw")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS raw.trips (trip_id VARCHAR, member_id VARCHAR, start_station_id VARCHAR,
                   end_station_id VARCHAR, started_at VARCHAR, ended_at VARCHAR, bike_type VARCHAR,
                   _loaded_at TIMESTAMP)""")
    if args.batch == 1:
        con.execute("DELETE FROM raw.trips")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.trips VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [r + [loaded_at] for r in new_trips])
    con.execute("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw.members (member_id VARCHAR, joined_on VARCHAR, plan VARCHAR,
                   updated_at TIMESTAMP, _loaded_at TIMESTAMP)""")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.members VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [r + [loaded_at] for r in member_rows])
    total = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM raw.trips").fetchone()[0]
    con.close()
    print(f"Batch {args.batch}: loaded {len(new_trips)} trips ({total} in raw.trips) and {len(member_rows)} members "
          f"into {args.db}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Sources, seeds and staging models
modules.summary: Declare raw tables as sources and check how fresh they are, load reference data as seeds, and write staging models that give everything downstream a clean start.

lessons.title: Sources and freshness
objectives: Declare sources and select from them with source()
Check source freshness
key_points: Sources declare the raw tables a project reads, in a YAML file under models, with a name, a schema and tables; models select from them with {{ source('raw', 'trips') }}, so lineage starts at the raw data and raw names live in one place.

Source freshness compares the newest value of a loaded_at_field, such as _loaded_at, with the current time: dbt source freshness reports PASS, WARN (after warn_after) or ERROR (after error_after) for each table.

Recent dbt versions take loaded_at_field and freshness under a source's or table's config, as in this course; older projects set them as top-level properties, and a table's setting overrides its source's.
Freshness checks catch the commonest data problem, a load that quietly stopped, before anyone reads yesterday's figures as today's; scheduled jobs run them before the build.
Describe sources, tables and columns in YAML: the descriptions appear in the generated documentation, and tests can be attached to source columns too.

lessons.title: Seeds
objectives: Load small reference data with seeds
Decide what should and shouldn't be a seed
key_points: A seed is a CSV file in the seeds folder that dbt seed loads into a table, for small, static reference data that belongs in version control, such as a list of stations or country codes.
Seeds aren't for raw data or anything large or changing often: that arrives through the ingestion tool, while a seed changes only when someone edits the file in git.
Models refer to a seed with ref('stations'), just like a model, so the seed joins the dependency graph and dbt build loads it before the models that use it.
dbt infers each seed column's type; set column_types in a properties file or dbt_project.yml where the guess matters, such as IDs with leading zeros or codes that look like numbers.
dbt seed reloads the CSV on every run (INSERT 12 for twelve rows); --full-refresh drops and recreates the table, which is needed when the CSV's columns change.

lessons.title: Staging models
objectives: Write a staging model for each source table
Keep staging models simple, consistent and safe for what's downstream
key_points: A staging model sits one-to-one on a source table: it renames columns, casts types, tidies values (lower-casing codes, trimming text) and converts units, and it's the only model that selects from that source.
Staging models don't join or aggregate; they give every later model the same clean starting point, so a change in the raw data is dealt with in one place.
Name them stg_<table> and materialise them as views, which are cheap and always current; write them as an import CTE (with source as (...)), then the changes, then a final select.
Keep raw columns that later models need, such as _loaded_at for incremental loads, and only drop rows that are never valid, such as exact duplicates.
List the columns explicitly rather than ending with select *, so a new or renamed raw column doesn't silently change every model downstream.

modules.title: Intermediate models, marts and Jinja
modules.summary: Layer business logic into intermediate models and marts, write reusable SQL with Jinja and macros, and select parts of the graph to build.

lessons.title: Layers: staging, intermediate and marts
objectives: Organise a project into staging, intermediate and mart layers
Give every model a clear grain
key_points: Projects are layered: staging models clean sources, intermediate models combine and reshape them with business logic, and marts present results for a use, such as a fact table of trips or a dashboard's daily table.

Intermediate models (int_) join, de-duplicate, pivot or compute logic that several marts reuse, such as a trip's duration and zones, so each rule is written once; they're usually views or ephemeral, and not shown to users.

Marts are what people query: facts (fct_), one row per event or transaction, and dimensions (dim_), one row per thing that describes events; build them as tables or incremental models so they're quick to read.
Every model should have one grain, what one row means, stated in its description and checked with a unique test on its key.
Which facts and dimensions a mart needs is a dimensional-modelling question, covered in depth in Data Warehousing and Dimensional Modelling; dbt is how such designs are usually built.

lessons.title: Jinja and macros
objectives: Use Jinja expressions, statements and context in models
Write a macro and call it from a model
key_points: Jinja is the template language dbt renders before the SQL runs: {{ ... }} outputs a value, {% ... %} runs logic such as if and for, and {# ... #} is a comment; dbt renders Jinja even inside SQL comments.
A macro is reusable Jinja in the macros folder, defined with {% macro name(args) %} ... {% endmacro %} and called like a function, such as {{ minutes_between('started_at', 'ended_at') }}.
dbt comes with cross-database macros such as dbt.datediff, dbt.dateadd and dbt.concat, which compile to each warehouse's own SQL, so macros built on them work with any adapter.
Useful context includes var('name') for project variables, target.name for the current target, env_var('NAME') for environment variables and this for the relation being built.
Packages such as dbt_utils add tested macros and generic tests: list them in packages.yml and install them with dbt deps.

lessons.title: Selecting and running parts of the graph
objectives: Select models with graph operators, paths, tags and state
Build safely with dbt build, --full-refresh and dbt retry
key_points: --select chooses what to run: a model name, +model (it and everything upstream), model+ (it and everything downstream), path:models/marts, tag:daily or test_type:unit; --exclude takes things out.
dbt ls --select ... lists what a selection matches without running anything, the safe way to check a selector before a big build.
dbt build runs seeds, models, snapshots and tests in DAG order, tests each model before the models that depend on it, and skips everything downstream of a failure.
state:modified, with --state pointing at an earlier run's manifest.json, selects only what has changed, which is how CI builds just the models a pull request touches.
--full-refresh rebuilds incremental models and seeds from scratch, and dbt retry reruns only what failed in the previous command.

-- Trips joined to their start and end stations, with each trip's duration. Intermediate models hold
-- reusable business logic; nothing outside the project reads them directly.
with trips as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_trips') }}
),

stations as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_stations') }}
)

select
    trips.trip_id,
    trips.member_id,
    trips.member_id is not null as is_member,
    trips.bike_type,
    trips.started_at,
    trips.ended_at,
    cast(trips.started_at as date) as trip_date,
    trips.start_station_id,
    start_station.zone as start_zone,
    trips.end_station_id,
    end_station.zone as end_zone,
    -- TODO: the trip's duration_minutes, using the minutes_between macro on started_at and ended_at
    null as duration_minutes,

modules.title: Testing and documenting
modules.summary: Catch bad data with generic and singular tests, check SQL logic with unit tests, and document the project with descriptions and a lineage graph.

lessons.title: Generic data tests
objectives: Attach generic tests to columns in YAML
Choose a test's severity, and read its failures
key_points: Data tests are SELECT queries that return the rows breaking a rule, and a test passes when it returns none; generic tests are attached to columns in YAML under data_tests (called tests before dbt 1.8).
dbt has four built-in generic tests: unique, not_null, accepted_values with a list of values, and relationships, which checks that every value exists in a column of another model, like a foreign key.
Recent dbt versions take a test's settings under arguments (such as values, or to and field) and options under config; severity: warn reports failures as a warning without failing the build.
Put unique and not_null on every model's key, accepted_values on codes and relationships on foreign keys; tests on staging catch problems early, and tests on marts guard what users see.
dbt test runs the tests; dbt build runs each model's tests straight after building it and skips its children when one fails; store_failures: true keeps the failing rows in a table to inspect.

lessons.title: Singular tests and unit tests
objectives: Write a singular test for a rule that generic tests can't express
Test a model's logic with a unit test on fixed inputs
key_points: A singular test is a .sql file in the tests folder with a query that returns bad rows, for rules that don't fit a generic test, such as no trip ending before it starts.
A custom generic test is a macro written with {% test name(model, column_name) %} ... {% endtest %}, which can then be attached to any column in YAML like the built-in tests.

Unit tests (dbt 1.8 and later) check a model's SQL on fixed inputs: under unit_tests in YAML, given lists mock rows for each ref or source, and expect lists the rows the model must return, with only the columns that matter.
Data tests check the data that arrived; unit tests check the code before any real data is involved, so they suit tricky logic such as durations, time zones and case expressions.
Give tests clear names and descriptions, so a failure in a CI log says which rule broke; a test's compiled SQL in target/compiled shows exactly what it checked.

lessons.title: Documentation and lineage
objectives: Document models and columns, and generate the documentation site
Use lineage, exposures and contracts to protect consumers
key_points: Descriptions of models, columns, sources and seeds go in YAML; a {% docs name %} block in a .md file holds longer text, used as description: '{{ doc("name") }}'.

dbt docs generate writes manifest.json (the project) and catalog.json (the warehouse's columns and types) to target/, and dbt docs serve opens a local site with every model's description, columns, SQL and tests.
The site's lineage graph shows how sources, seeds and models connect, so you can see what a change affects and where a number comes from.

Exposures declare what uses the project, such as a dashboard or a machine learning pipeline, with an owner; they appear in the lineage graph and can be selected, as in dbt build --select +exposure:station_dashboard.
A model contract (contract: enforced: true, with a data_type for each column) makes dbt check the model's columns and types when it builds; Data Quality, Testing and Data Contracts goes further.

modules.title: Snapshots, incremental models and CI
modules.summary: Keep the history of changing rows with snapshots, build large tables incrementally, and run dbt in CI and production.

lessons.title: Snapshots
objectives: Explain how snapshots record changes over time
Configure a snapshot with the timestamp strategy
key_points: A snapshot records how mutable rows change: each run compares the source with the snapshot table and, for a changed row, closes the old version (sets dbt_valid_to) and inserts the new one, a type 2 slowly changing dimension.
Snapshot tables add dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to (null for the current version), dbt_scd_id and dbt_updated_at; a row's current version is the one whose dbt_valid_to is null.
The timestamp strategy spots changes from an updated_at column and is the most reliable; the check strategy compares the values of chosen columns (check_cols) when there's no trustworthy timestamp.

Since dbt 1.9, snapshots can be defined in YAML with a relation, such as source('raw', 'members'), and a config with unique_key, strategy and updated_at; older projects use {% snapshot %} blocks in .sql files.

A snapshot only sees changes when it runs, so run dbt snapshot at least as often as the source changes; a value that changes and changes back between runs is never recorded, and lost history can't be rebuilt.

lessons.title: Incremental models
objectives: Build a large table incrementally, safely
Handle late-arriving rows and changes to the model
key_points: An incremental model builds the whole table on its first run, then on later runs processes only new or changed rows and adds them, which saves time and money on large event tables.
In the model, {% if is_incremental() %} wraps the filter for new rows and compares with the existing table through {{ this }}, such as where _loaded_at > (select max(_loaded_at) from {{ this }}).

unique_key makes reruns safe: with the delete+insert or merge strategies, rows whose key is already in the table are replaced rather than duplicated, while append just adds rows; which strategies exist depends on the adapter.
Filter on when rows were loaded, or re-read a lookback window, rather than on when events happened: a trip from yesterday that arrives late is missed by where trip_date > (select max(trip_date) ...).

dbt build --full-refresh rebuilds an incremental model from scratch, as needed after its logic changes; on_schema_change sets what happens when columns change (ignore, fail, append_new_columns or sync_all_columns).
dbt 1.9 added the microbatch strategy, which processes time-series data in batches of an event_time column and can reprocess a chosen range of batches.

lessons.title: Running dbt in CI and production
objectives: Set up targets and a CI job for a dbt project
Build only what changed with state selection
key_points: Use separate targets: developers build into their own schema or file, CI into a throwaway one, and production jobs with --target prod, so testing never touches what users read.
Run dbt build in CI on every pull request, with pinned versions of dbt-core and the adapter, so broken SQL, failing tests and invalid YAML are caught before merging.

Slim CI builds only what changed: keep production's manifest.json and run dbt build --select state:modified+ --state path/to/prod-artifacts, with --defer so unchanged parents are read from production.

Every run writes artifacts to target/: manifest.json (the project and its graph), run_results.json (what ran, for how long and how it ended) and, after docs generate, catalog.json; tools and later runs read them.

Production runs are scheduled by an orchestrator such as Airflow or Dagster, or by dbt's hosted platform, typically dbt source freshness, then dbt build, then dbt docs generate, with alerts on failure.

# GitHub Actions: build and test the whole project on every pull request and every push to main.

project.title: Model a football club's ticket sales
project.brief: A football club wants trustworthy figures on ticket sales, attendance and its fans for each home match. Load its synthetic data with make_club_data.py (raw.matches, raw.ticket_sales and raw.fans in club.duckdb, plus a sections.csv seed), then build a dbt project from scratch: sources with freshness checks, the seed, staging models, an intermediate model for sales, and marts including an incremental fct_ticket_sales, dim_matches, dim_fans built on a snapshot of the fans, and a match-attendance mart with revenue net of refunds and the share of each section's capacity sold. The raw data has the usual problems: a sale delivered twice, a negative price, and refunds that arrive later as new rows. Load batch 2 to prove that the incremental model and the snapshot handle new sales, late refunds and fans changing tier, and add a CI workflow.
deliverables: The dbt project: dbt_project.yml, profiles.yml with dev and ci targets, sources, seed, models, macros, tests and snapshot
Tests: unique and not_null keys, accepted_values and relationships where they fit, at least one singular test (for example, no section sold beyond its capacity) and at least one unit test
Model and column descriptions, an exposure for the club's attendance dashboard, and the output of dbt docs generate
The output of dbt build after batch 1, and of dbt snapshot and dbt build after batch 2, with counts showing the incremental model and snapshot are right
A GitHub Actions workflow that builds the project on the ci target
A README explaining the layers, the grain of each mart, and how to run the project

rubric.name: Correct marts
rubric.description: Duplicates and invalid prices are handled, refunds reduce revenue, and attendance and capacity shares match the data.

rubric.name: Project structure
rubric.description: Sources, staging, intermediate and marts are layered cleanly, with ref and source used throughout, sensible materialisations and a macro where logic repeats.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: Generic tests on keys and codes, meaningful singular and unit tests, and severities chosen deliberately; dbt build passes.

rubric.name: History and incremental loads
rubric.description: The fans snapshot keeps tier changes, and fct_ticket_sales picks up new sales and late refunds without duplicates; a full refresh gives the same result.

rubric.name: Documentation and CI
rubric.description: Models and columns are described, the exposure appears in the lineage, the workflow builds on the ci target, and the README is clear.

project.submit: Paste your project files (each with its path), the dbt build, snapshot and count outputs for both batches, your workflow and your README. A link to a repository is welcome too.

files.content:
"""Load a football club's synthetic ticketing data into the raw schema of club.duckdb, in two batches.

    python make_club_data.py             batch 1: five home matches, their ticket sales, and the fans table
    python make_club_data.py --batch 2   batch 2: the sixth match's sales, refunds for earlier ones, tier changes

raw.matches and raw.fans are replaced with the source's current state; raw.ticket_sales is appended to. Every
row has _loaded_at. Only random.random() is used, so every computer gets the same data.
"""

import argparse
import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import duckdb

SECTIONS = ["N1", "N2", "E1", "E2", "S1", "S2", "W1", "W2"]
MATCHES = [("H01", "2024-08-17 19:00:00", "League", "Riverside Rovers"), ("H02", "2024-08-31 16:00:00", "League", "Northgate Town"),
           ("H03", "2024-09-14 19:00:00", "Cup", "Harbour City"), ("H04", "2024-09-28 16:00:00", "League", "Valley United"),
           ("H05", "2024-10-19 19:00:00", "League", "Old Mill Athletic"), ("H06", "2024-11-02 16:00:00", "League", "Castle Park")]


def fans(rng, batch):
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, 801):
        tier = "season" if rng.random() < 0.3 else "member" if rng.random() < 0.6 else "casual"
        joined = datetime(2019, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=int(rng.random() * 2000))
        rows.append([f"F{i:04d}", f"{joined:%Y-%m-%d}", tier, f"{joined:%Y-%m-%d} 00:00:00"])
    if batch == 2:
        for r in rows[10::40]:  # some fans move tier after the October match
            r[2] = {"casual": "member", "member": "season", "season": "member"}[r[2]]
            r[3] = "2024-10-25 10:00:00"
    return rows


def sales(rng, matches, first_id):
    rows, n = [], first_id
    for match_id, kick_off, competition, _opponent in matches:
        ko = datetime.fromisoformat(kick_off)
        for _ in range(900 + int(rng.random() * 400) + (300 if competition == "Cup" else 0)):
            sold = ko - timedelta(minutes=int(rng.random() * 30 * 24 * 60))
            section = SECTIONS[int(rng.random() * len(SECTIONS))]
            price = {"N": 28, "E": 35, "S": 28, "W": 45}[section[0]] - (6 if section[1] == "2" else 0)
            rows.append([f"K{n:07d}", match_id, f"F{int(rng.random() * 800) + 1:04d}", section, f"{price:.2f}",
                         f"{sold:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}", "online" if rng.random() < 0.7 else "box office", "sold"])
            n += 1
    return rows


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--batch", type=int, choices=[1, 2], default=1)
    parser.add_argument("--db", default="club.duckdb")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    batch1 = sales(random.Random(11), MATCHES[:5], 1)
    batch1.append(batch1[40][:])  # one sale delivered twice
    batch1[99][4] = "-28.00"  # a negative price from a till error
    if args.batch == 1:
        new_sales = batch1  # the sixth match is already in the fixture list, with no sales yet
    else:
        new_sales = sales(random.Random(12), MATCHES[5:], len(batch1) + 1)
        for row in batch1[200:215]:  # refunds for an earlier match arrive as new rows with status refunded
            new_sales.append(row[:7] + ["refunded"])
    loaded_at = datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)
    con = duckdb.connect(args.db)
    con.execute("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS raw")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS raw.ticket_sales (ticket_id VARCHAR, match_id VARCHAR, fan_id VARCHAR,
                   section_id VARCHAR, price VARCHAR, sold_at VARCHAR, channel VARCHAR, status VARCHAR,
                   _loaded_at TIMESTAMP)""")
    if args.batch == 1:
        con.execute("DELETE FROM raw.ticket_sales")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.ticket_sales VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [r + [loaded_at] for r in new_sales])
    con.execute("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw.matches (match_id VARCHAR, kick_off TIMESTAMP, competition VARCHAR,
                   opponent VARCHAR, _loaded_at TIMESTAMP)""")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.matches VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [list(m) + [loaded_at] for m in MATCHES])
    con.execute("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw.fans (fan_id VARCHAR, joined_on VARCHAR, tier VARCHAR,
                   updated_at TIMESTAMP, _loaded_at TIMESTAMP)""")
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.fans VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [r + [loaded_at] for r in fans(random.Random(13), args.batch)])
    total = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM raw.ticket_sales").fetchone()[0]
    con.close()
    print(f"Batch {args.batch}: loaded {len(new_sales)} ticket rows ({total} in raw.ticket_sales) into {args.db}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
